introduction: These readings take the vocabulary of war and turn it inside out. Bahá’u’lláh forbids contention and calls for conquest of hearts by wisdom and utterance; ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says that this army's swords give life where the others kill, that its hosts are the angels of the Concourse, that physical warfare bears no fruit, and that the real hero is the one who overcomes the self. All thirteen quotations are read here beside thirteen from elsewhere. Ten stand alongside: Paul's armour and weapons 'not carnal', the word sharper than a sword, Zechariah's 'not by might', Elisha's chariots of fire, Blake's mental fight, Proverbs and the Dhammapada on self-conquest. Three add a caution or a contrast: the Qur'an's rule for actual fighting, Mark Twain's War Prayer on what martial piety asks for, and Heraclitus, who thought war the father of all.
questions: Why keep the language of armies and swords at all, if the meaning is its opposite?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá says that sword killed and this one gives life. Name the weapons the readings allow.
Twain shows what is hidden in a prayer for victory. What is the risk in speaking of faith as a battle, and how do the readings guard against it?
'He who overcomes the self' is called the righteous one. Why is that the hardest campaign?

outside.why: Paul tells the Ephesians to take the whole armour of God, and having done all, to stand.
The Qur'an permits fighting those who fight you, and forbids beginning hostilities. These readings turn 'war' wholly into a figure: what is gained, and what must be guarded?
Paul says that the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty to the pulling down of strong holds.
Hebrews calls the word of God quick and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword.
Isaiah foresees swords beaten into plowshares, and nations learning war no more.
Elisha's servant had his eyes opened, and saw the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire.
Zechariah hears: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the Lord of hosts.
Blake vowed: I will not cease from mental fight, nor shall my sword sleep in my hand.
Mark Twain wrote a prayer that says aloud what a prayer for victory asks: help us to tear their soldiers to bloody shreds. What are the risks of speaking of faith in the language of battle?
Heraclitus called war the father of all and the king of all. Is physical warfare as fruitless as the reading says?
Proverbs says that he that ruleth his spirit is better than he that taketh a city.
The Dhammapada says that one who conquers himself is a greater conqueror than one who conquers a thousand men in battle.
A psalm promises: the Lord shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in.
